Experiments that changed questions

Bandura and the Bobo doll

Children who watched an adult hit an inflatable doll imitated it, even with new gestures and phrases.

In 1961, Albert Bandura and colleagues at Stanford brought children aged 3 to 6 into a playroom. Some watched an adult punch, kick and toss an inflatable clown doll called Bobo, while saying things like "Pow!". Others watched an adult play quietly.

Learning by watching

When the children were later left alone with the doll, those who had seen the aggressive adult were much more likely to attack it, copying specific actions such as hitting it with a mallet or repeating the same phrases. In later studies, seeing someone rewarded or punished changed how much they imitated.

The experiment supports social learning theory: we learn by watching others, without needing direct rewards. Critics have noted that Bobo is a doll designed to be hit, so not all of it was real aggression. Even so, it strongly influenced the debate on media violence.

References

  1. Bandura, A., Ross, D. y Ross, S. A. (1961). Transmission of aggression through imitation of aggressive models. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 63(3), 575–582.
